highlights.quote: Aggression is a useful word only when it is made to carry less.
highlights.judgment: The book's governing move stated with unusual economy; the definitional chapter earns the rest of the volume.

highlights.quote: The bones establish a violent meeting; they do not identify its command.
highlights.judgment: Exemplary epistemic discipline about what each class of evidence can bear — and also the book's most over-used sentence shape.

highlights.quote: A valley emptied of houses is not a written confession.
highlights.judgment: Concrete, memorable formulation of the archaeological caution; craft at its best.

highlights.quote: A person may strike in anger. A household may raid. A state may punish. An army may wage war. A regime may organise atrocity. The hand can be similar; the world directing it is not.
highlights.judgment: Strong thesis statement, but the anaphoric ladder plus antithetical closer is a template repeated at many chapter ends.

highlights.quote: The iron did not organise itself.
highlights.judgment: Effective aphoristic close, though the book reaches for this cadence too reliably in final position.

highlights.quote: The first bones had come from the riverbank in 1997, when an amateur archaeologist named Detlef Jantzen found a human upper-arm bone with a flint arrowhead embedded in it.
highlights.judgment: Internal inconsistency: Jantzen is introduced pages earlier as the professional directing the 2009 trench, so the same name carries two incompatible identities.

highlights.quote: A man named Muhammad, a clerk from the quarter near the Friday mosque, would have seen the heaps form beside the irrigation channels
highlights.judgment: Named invented individuals in a nonfiction reconstruction; the conditional verb only half-flags the fabrication, and elsewhere (Rābiʿa at the bakery) it is not flagged at all.

highlights.quote: The past leaves constraints; people still decide what those constraints will permit.
highlights.judgment: A genuinely earned ending that resolves the fifteen-chapter argument rather than merely summarising it.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Every chapter opens with a cinematic, present-tense-feeling reconstructed scene (a hand, an object, a moment of contact) before the analysis begins.
instances: The trowel struck something that was not stone.
The copper helmet came off the skull in Leonard Woolley’s hand.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Verdicts are delivered as a negation-antithesis couplet — 'X establishes A; it does not establish B' / 'X is not Y'.
instances: The bones establish a violent meeting; they do not identify its command.
A valley emptied of houses is not a written confession.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Chapters end on a short aphoristic closer that names an object and hands it the moral.
instances: The iron did not organise itself.
At Girsu, Eannatum supplied all three, and the vultures carried the result into stone.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Anaphoric ladders of institutional actors ('A wall… A ration… A boundary…') used to convert the argument into cadence.
instances: A wall required commands before it could protect. A ration required a clerk before it could feed. A boundary required a claimant before it could become a reason for war.
A person may strike in anger. A household may raid. A state may punish. An army may wage war. A regime may organise atrocity. The hand can be similar; the world directing it is not.

recurringPatterns.pattern: Paired case comparison announced by a formulaic hinge sentence that states the two sites share a form but not a setting or separate two fused questions.
instances: Crow Creek and Talheim therefore share a form without sharing a historical setting.
Uruk and Mohenjo-daro separate two questions often fused together.

summary: A genuinely accomplished comparative history of human aggression whose thesis — that the hand is similar and the institutions directing it are not — is stated early, tested against fifteen very different evidentiary regimes, and answered rather than merely restated at the end. Its greatest strength is source discipline: the book repeatedly says what bones, sagas, tax registers, coroner's files and royal inscriptions can and cannot support, and it refuses false symmetry between counted and uncounted societies. Prose is concrete and largely free of stock AI diction, with real sentence-level craft in the archaeological and administrative passages. The weaknesses are architectural rather than local: every chapter runs the same circuit (cinematic opening scene, document, paired comparison, aphoristic institutional closer), and the antithesis couplet and anaphoric ladder appear so often that by the later chapters the argument's rhythm is predictable before its content is. Two integrity problems need attention — the Jantzen identity contradiction in Chapter 1, and the named invented individuals (Muhammad the clerk, Rābiʿa in the bakery) inside otherwise scrupulous nonfiction reconstruction. Pacing also sags in the long middle chapters, where several fully specified comparisons make the same point about offices and classification.
